newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Waco film may shed light on McVeigh motives.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Waco film may shed light on McVeigh motives.

text.p: Most Americans think of Waco as the Texas city where a fire engulfed suicidal Branch Davidian cultists in a 1993 horrow show, killing 76 and ending a 51-day siege by federal agents.

Two years to the day after cult leader David Koresh and most of his followers perished, Timothy McVeigh made sure Waco never faded from memory, marking the April 19 anniversary by murdering 168 people in the Oklahoma City bombing.

For four years since Waco, conspiracy theorists have spun yarns accusing the government of covering up "what really happened." Waco has become a "Who killed Kennedy?" for the 1990s, helping those who believe U.N. black helicopters are patrolling America's heartland spread their gospel.

McVeigh's defense attorneys at the bombing trial in Denver portrayed their now-doomed client as a believer in such theories, beliefs that they said transformed the ex-Army gunner into an anti-government crusader.

Now, everything we know or think we know about Waco and conspiracy may change as charges of a government cover-up move from Internet home pages to the arthouse cinema. A new documentary film, "Waco: The Rules of Engagement," has changed some perceptions.

Since its debut at Robert Redford's Sundance festival in January, the nearly three-hour work, which opened the Human Rights Watch International Film Festival in New York, has toured the country, challenging assertions by the Justice Department and Attorney General Janet Reno that Davidians, not government agents, burned their compound and shot one another.
FILM ASKS MOTIVATION FOR WACO RAID

The filmmakers are anxious to separate themselves from anti-government types who may use the documentary to promote their theories, but they also feel they need to promote what they believe is an important film.

"What McVeigh did was reprehensible, but why haven't the mainstream media and federal officials questioned Waco? One of the things we tried to accomplish in the film was to ask what was the motivation for doing the Waco raid," said Dan Gifford, a former CNN newsman who with his wife Ann Sommer-Gifford is the film's executive producer.
"It is important not to be weary of the truth. We gathered the facts for individuals to decide, hoping our film can facilitate a lucid conversation," Sommer-Gifford said.

The literal smoking gun that lies at the core of the film is a never-before-seen FBI surveillance video shot from the skies two miles (3.2 km) above the Davidian compound when the government raid began on April 19, 1993.

The film contends that the infrared, black-and-white videotape shows government agents firing automatic weapons at the compound after it was engulfed in flames. The FBI told congressional panels not one shot was fired during the 51-day siege except for gas meant to flush out the cultists and free 25 children, who eventually perished, from their alleged abusers. The film also says the government use of CS gas accidentally ignited the Davidian home in the first place.
GUNFIRE OR REFLECTIONS FROM THE GROUND?

The government disputes these charges, saying the heat-sensitive tapes simply show reflections from the ground and in no way depict agents firing at the encampment. These denials were backed up by most of a dozen experts assembled by The Washington Post newspaper for a separate analysis although four of the experts said the ground bursts could be gunfire.

The documentary highlights testimony by Edward Allard, an ex-Army expert on Forward-Looking Infrared or FLIR technology, who says the flashes from the ground are indicative of gunfire even though the gunners are hard to see.

"Waco" tantalizes conspiracy theorists with the notion the FBI and others attacked the Davidians in an act of police vigilantism to avenge the deaths of four Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms (ATF) agents slain during the botched raid that started the standoff on Feb. 28 of that year. "Look at the record on that, not one of the ATF agents made an original report ... the FBI covered up evidence," Gifford said.

The documentary also features audio-taped conversations between Koresh and federal negotiators, congressional footage from CNN and C-SPAN and disturbing visuals, one of which shows the charred remains of burned children.

McVeigh and Waco could be the chicken and the egg riddle of all time. Would McVeigh have been motivated to kill if Koresh's flock had not died? Or was McVeigh a loose cannon, schooled in warfare by the Army and itching for a chance to put into action a far-right manifesto?

But the Giffords say that is not the issue. "If we don't learn from the past we are condemned to repeat it. This certain group of people (Davidians) were villified and the people in control dehumanized them," Sommer-Gifford said.
